scope: Eight unselected Books 10–16 canonical lesson drafts; source sense, seven-step pedagogy, bilingual fidelity, answer grounding, target detector, transfer and originality
buildCheck: Independent focused build and --check pass: 8 lessons, 48 questions, 32 audio requests, zero structural flags.
originalityScreen: Compared 192 learner-facing English strings with 2,604 source examples: 9 six-token overlaps in the target expressions and no apparent copied source clause outside target wording. This mechanical screen does not certify originality.

lessonReviews.note: The demanding qualification criteria are explicit; the lesson does not equate a high bar with impossibility. Four replies and writing transfer are grounded.
The lesson repeatedly attributes plural 'clothes' becoming too small on evidence about only one named garment; see R4047-01.
The target detector admits subject–verb disagreement under live case-insensitive matching, and writing model 2 infers a stable priority from a single coat choice; see R4051-01 and R4051-02.
A repeated group replacement habit, usable goods and concrete reuse alternatives distinguish throwaway culture from a one-off safety disposal.
Physical items and an untested idea are distinct, viable contexts for cast aside. Reply/scene/dialogue keys are supported by the stated facts.
The sustained change is well grounded, but one reply option uses redundant English wording; see R4061-01.
Interest stimulated by repeated previews is distinguished from purchase or registration; the source and assessed target forms match.
Shared overall direction and specific material differences are preserved in the scenarios and both writing models.

findings.issue: The lesson teaches 'grow out of clothes' as a plural wardrobe claim, but the listening supplies only one school jumper, the scene only one raincoat, and each writing model only one shirt or coat. A single undersized garment does not by itself establish that the child has grown out of their clothes generally. The scene key also calls a single raincoat 'the clothes'.
findings.recommendedRepair: Give each learner-facing situation at least two once-fitting garments now too small, or narrow the target to singular garment forms and update source/assessment ownership accordingly. Preserve EN/ZH, source expression and exact spans.

findings.issue: The second regex branch includes '[A-Z][a-z]+' while runtime uses case-insensitive flags, so it also matches plural pronouns with singular 'attaches'.
findings.evidence: Live case-insensitive positives include ungrammatical 'importance they attaches to fashion', 'importance we attaches to fashion', and 'importance people attaches to fashion'.
findings.recommendedRepair: Constrain singular subjects without a broad case-insensitive capitalized-name branch, or use bounded explicit assessed names, and test source and legitimate singular/plural positives plus these three negatives.

findings.issue: Model 2 compares one repairable-coat purchase with one new-season design purchase, then concludes that the importance assigned to fashion differs. Its own contrast task says a single receipt cannot establish a buyer's reasons or competing priorities; model 2 gives no stated ranking or repeated pattern.
findings.recommendedRepair: Add explicit preference interviews or repeated ranked decisions for the two families, and align the Traditional Chinese and any changed glossary spans.

findings.issue: 'A repair-minded mindset has taken hold' is a redundant 'minded mindset' phrase in the golden reply. The Chinese can stay natural but should track a natural English answer.
findings.recommendedRepair: Use 'A repair mindset has taken hold in the team' or another concise target-bearing formulation, with faithful Traditional Chinese.
